title: The Reparations Bill: What the Caribbean Is Asking Britain For | Across the Water, Ep. 2
lede: Commonwealth leaders are meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, and Caribbean governments have made reparations for slavery the headline issue. In 1833 Britain paid £20 million, about 40% of government spending, to slave owners, not the enslaved. This episode explains what the Caribbean is asking for, the estimates of what repair would cost, and where London now stands.
keyPoints: CHOGM 2026 runs Nov 1–4 in St John's, Antigua and Barbuda; the CARICOM Reparations Commission calls it the "reparations CHOGM."
After the Slavery Abolition Act 1833, Britain paid £20 million to slave owners, about 40% of government spending that year; the loan was finally repaid in 2015 (Full Fact).
In March 2026 the UN General Assembly declared the transatlantic slave trade the gravest crime against humanity: 123 in favour, 3 against, 52 abstentions, including the UK.

A 2023 Brattle Group report for the University of the West Indies estimated reparations at $100–131 trillion, including about $24 trillion from Britain. These are estimates no government has accepted.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he is open to a formal apology but has ruled out reparation payments, offering debt help instead: longer repayment and lower interest rates.
King Charles told the summit on Nov 3 that the slave trade fills his soul with "the most profound personal sorrow," but did not apologise.
